summary:
Consensual same-sex intimacy was criminalised in Mongolia's Criminal Code of 1961 and decriminalised in 1993, when all references were removed. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation.

Protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is spread across several instruments rather than a single equality statute. Section 14.1.1 of the Penal Code, in force since 1 July 2017, prohibits discrimination on both grounds. Article 6 of the Labour Code, in force since 2022, prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression. Article 1.3.2 of the revised Criminal Law adopted on 3 December 2015 bars discrimination in criminalisation and sentencing on grounds including sexual and gender orientation. No comprehensive equality law is in place.

Hate-crime and hate-speech provisions cover gender identity. The Criminal Code adopted on 3 December 2015 included gender identity and sexual orientation as protected grounds for hate crimes; it was scheduled to take effect on 1 September 2016 and was postponed to 1 July 2017. Section 10(1)(2)(14) of the Penal Code aggravates penalties for homicides motivated by hate towards the victim's gender identity or sexual orientation, and hate speech on the basis of gender identity is outlawed.

Transgender visitors and residents may change their legal gender on birth certificates or citizen identification cards following sex reassignment surgery, under a June 2009 amendment to Article 20(1) of the Civil Registration Law.

Marriage is defined in Article 16(11) of the Constitution as a union of a man and a woman. Same-sex relationships are not recognised and same-sex couple households are ineligible for the state protections afforded to opposite-sex couples. No union recognition of any kind is available.

Enforcement of hate-crime provisions remains weak in documented practice. As of August 2018 the LGBT Centre had trained more than 300 police officers, prosecutors and judges on handling hate crimes, and a 2019 report indicates training reached over 500 officers, prosecutors and judges. Following an officer's assault on a detained transgender woman, reported in October 2019, the LGBT Center trained police on the 2017 criminal code's hate-crime provisions and the force adopted guidelines requiring officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender regardless of identity documents. Despite this training, local reports and activists say police continue to disregard or not take seriously complaints of hate crimes against LGBTQ people, and attacks often result in no punishment.

Documented anti-trans violence includes a September 2009 incident in which a hyper-nationalist group kidnapped three transgender women in broad daylight at a Ulaanbaatar promenade, drove them to a cemetery, beat and sexually assaulted them, and forced them to perform sexual acts; the attack was not reported to police. The most recent documented case in this record is from February 2014, when a gay man was sexually assaulted by a neo-Nazi group; no later incident is documented here. Violence and discrimination against LGBTQ people are reported as often unreported to police for fear of victimisation and reprisal.

Survey data is dated and not trans-specific: a 2012 National Human Rights Commission survey of LGBT people found almost 80% had experienced broadly categorised 'human-rights abuse' in the preceding three years, with the window closing in 2012. A 2019 report found 79% of LGBTQ-identified young people had experienced bullying, discrimination or ostracism. A 2013 report found over 73% of LGBTQ Mongolians had considered suicide due to social non-acceptance.

As of June 2014, the law provided no additional penalty for bias-motivated violence and no requirement for law enforcement to record a suspected bias motive; a January 2014 draft adding hate-bias motive as an aggravating factor was replaced in late May 2014 by generalised discrimination references. Later enactments, dated above, added gender-identity and sexual-orientation hate-crime grounds.

Groups can register. Mongolian culture is described as strongly heteronormative, and despite the 2017 protections, ostracism, harassment and violence persist socially and systemically.
tangentialFactors:
The 2008 social scene is described as having virtually no presence, venues or activism, with two organisations holding furtive monthly parties where attendees feared being outed. This account is from 2008 and no later assessment of venue presence is on record.

A December 2018 social experiment in Ulaanbaatar placed three LGBTQ people, including a transgender man, roadside to observe reactions; online responses ranged from death threats to positive comments, and the account states the public was more welcoming of the lesbian and the trans man than of the gay man.

The sex education curriculum introduced in 1998 includes discussion of LGBTQ and sexual health issues, though teachers may choose whether to cover these topics.

The Establishment profiled Anaraa Nyamdorj, a trans man and co-founder/advisor of the LGBT Centre, who came out in 2004 and began transition in 2011, describing transition access and acceptance in Ulaanbaatar around the 2018 Pride.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source finding is on record from the Asian Development Bank's legal-status review for Mongolia; that gap is unresolved rather than a finding of absence.

The inventory contains no entry, visa, or border-screening rules for transgender travellers to Mongolia, and no documentation on how gender markers on foreign passports are treated at Mongolian entry points. This is not sourced either way.

The inventory does not document access to gender-affirming care for visitors, restroom or facility rules, or any trans-specific violence in Mongolia after February 2014; the most recent documented incident in this record is from 2014, and no later instance is documented.

Survey figures cited (2012, 2013, 2019) measure LGBT-wide populations rather than trans people specifically, and their collection windows closed years ago; they are not current trans-specific prevalence.
